title: TV buyer's guide for the holidays: OLED, micro RGB, QNED, LCD?!

blocks.text: Buying a TV used to be very straightforward. In the past, knowing how far your couch was from the television mount was enough information to determine how many screen inches your TV should be. In these modern times, that is no longer the case. The LCD panel of yore has evolved into its different iterations – from LED, OLED, micro RGB, to having different types of finishes (such as matte!), to resolutions like 4K and 8K, and AI assistant functions. The living room TV has evolved from being just a living room entertainment hub, into a full blown home command center.
This is a guide to help dispel and educate what kind of TV you should be buying for your living room.

It is important to note that different brands use a lot of marketing jargon. While consumer electronics marketing often relies on proprietary branding, the premium market fundamentally divides into three primary display philosophies: Self-Emissive Displays (OLED) , Dedicated Primary Color Micro Emitters (Micro RGB / Mini RGB) , and Quantum-Enhanced Backlit LCDs (QNED / Mini-LED). At the recent holiday event from LG Electronics, they showcased different use cases for each type.

Every consumer television creates an image through the precise interplay of illumination and chrominance. However, the mechanical method by which light is generated and manipulated dictates things like black levels, color saturation, off-axis viewing stability, and peak luminance.

Self-emissive Organic Light-Emitting Diode (OLED) technology functions without an external backlight unit. In an OLED panel, every individual sub-pixel produces its own light and color, allowing each pixel to be dimmed or completely turned off independently of its neighbors.

Because inactive pixels produce zero light output, self-emissive displays deliver true black levels and infinite native contrast. In scenes featuring high dynamic contrast—such as bright city lights against a midnight sky or starfields in deep space—there is no light bleeding or haloing (“blooming”) into surrounding dark areas. This pixel-level control provides an image that remains the reference standard for color grading suites and film directors.

This simply means that OLED technology is best for true cinephiles who want to enjoy a film the way a director intended it. Blooming effects can get out of hand especially with white subtitles, and for people with astigmatism. Sometimes when viewing YouTube videos or playing certain video games, you can never get a true “black” screen in horror films or scenes that portray dark areas unless you are watching on an OLED display.
Why choose Micro RGB and Mini RGB

Micro RGB and Mini RGB architectures represent a major advancement in solid-state lighting and color science. Rather than utilizing standard blue LEDs coated with yellow phosphor or shining a broad-spectrum white backlight through subtractive color filters, Micro RGB displays employ microscopic, dedicated primary red, green, and blue light sources.

By generating primary light directly at the emitter stage, Micro RGB technology achieves an extraordinary degree of spectral accuracy. In traditional filtered LCDs or standard phosphor-driven panels, driving high peak brightness can wash out delicate hues, causing deep crimsons, emerald greens, and rich cyans to shift toward white. Micro RGB eliminates this color clipping, maintaining full chromatic saturation and spectral purity across the entire brightness curve.

Micro RGB is best for people who like to use their TV as an art centerpiece. There have been times when photos displayed on Micro RGB are mistaken to be mounted photos — because the colors look and feel that way. Micro RGB is also great for gamers that want to experience a wide gamut of crisp colors when they play. A high refresh rate screen usually accompanies this, such as the C6 series.

Quantum Nano-Emitting Diode (QNED) and Mini-LED displays represent the pinnacle of liquid crystal display (LCD) engineering. Unlike legacy direct-lit or edge-lit screens that rely on dozens of large LED modules, Mini-LED backlights employ thousands of miniaturized LED chips arranged in an ultra-dense array behind the LCD panel, controlled across hundreds or thousands of independent local dimming zones.

QNED technology is great for studios and family rooms that let in a lot of light. Imagine a studio that has a strong key light shining directly at the host with a TV in the background. A regular TV would have a lot of glare. QNED technology removes that hassle to make the viewing experience better.

One of the eye-catching fascinations of the new generation of LG evo AI TV’s is the AI Magic Remote that automatically customizes according to the user’s voice. That would mean having different profiles at home depending on who is using the remote control without having to switch users.

This is a basic guide to the different screen technologies available in the market today. Consumers can mix and match features depending on budget and needs because these days, there’s a TV for everyone!
